subject: Young planets colliding
caption: Two young rocky planets about to collide in a dusty disc around a young star, in a NASA artist's concept of the violent era when Earth was built.
note: Painted for a planetary system around a pair of distant stars, not the early Solar System; a stand-in for Earth's era of giant impacts.

subject: Late Heavy Bombardment
caption: Comets and asteroids pound the young Moon, scarring it with the craters still seen on its face today.
note: Whether a sharp 'late heavy bombardment' spike happened about 3.9 billion years ago is now debated; many scientists favour a slower decline in impacts. Portrait format, with a small artist's credit in a corner.

subject: Lava erupting under the sea
caption: Glowing lava breaks out on the deep sea floor at the West Mata volcano near Tonga today, a modern analogue for the volcanic sea floors of the young Earth.
note: Present-day photo from a deep-sea vehicle, whose basket shows at the bottom edge.

subject: Jack Hills, Western Australia
caption: The Jack Hills of Western Australia seen from orbit today; zircon crystals in their rocks are the oldest known pieces of Earth, about 4.4 billion years old.
note: The rocks of the hills are Archean; only tiny zircon grains inside them date from the Hadean. Satellite view, square.

subject: Acasta Gneiss
caption: A banded piece of the Acasta Gneiss from northern Canada, at about 4 billion years one of the oldest rocks on Earth.
note: Small file (1024 px). The oldest parts are about 4.03 billion years old, right at the Hadean-Archean boundary.

subject: Living stromatolites, Lake Thetis
caption: Stromatolites on the shore of Lake Thetis in Western Australia today, a modern analogue of the microbial mounds that were among Earth's first signs of life.
note: Present-day photo standing in for the Archean.

subject: Stromatolites under water, Shark Bay
caption: A snorkeller glides over living stromatolites in Shark Bay, Western Australia, a modern analogue of the shallow Archean sea floor.
credit: Ed Landing and Markes E. Johnson
note: Present-day photo; the swimmer gives scale.

subject: Banded iron formation, Barberton
caption: Red and grey layers of a banded iron formation from the Barberton Greenstone Belt of South Africa, laid down in Archean seas over 3 billion years ago.
note: Hand specimen with a ruler at the edge.
imageDateLabel: Rock formed over 3 billion years ago

subject: Archean pillow lava
caption: Rounded pillows of Archean lava, about 2.7 billion years old, in Michigan; they formed when lava erupted under water.
imageDateLabel: Lava erupted about 2.7 billion years ago

subject: Banded iron gorge, Karijini
caption: Kalmina Gorge in Karijini National Park, Western Australia, cut through layered banded iron rock laid down around 2.5 billion years ago, when oxygen first built up.
note: Present-day photo; the rocks belong to the Hamersley Group, at the Archean-Proterozoic boundary.
imageDateLabel: Present day · rocks about 2.5 billion years old

subject: Grypania
caption: Coiled ribbons of Grypania, one of the oldest fossils visible to the naked eye and possibly an early alga.
note: Grypania fossils range from about 1.9 to 1.4 billion years old; the age of this slab is not stated, and what Grypania was is still debated.

subject: Belt Supergroup stromatolites
caption: Columns of fossil stromatolites in limestone beside the Going-to-the-Sun Road in Glacier National Park, built by microbes about 1.4 billion years ago.

subject: Bass Limestone stromatolites, Grand Canyon
caption: Wavy layers of fossil stromatolites in the Bass Limestone deep in the Grand Canyon, about 1.25 billion years old.

subject: Kimberella on a microbial mat
caption: A museum model of the Ediacaran sea floor, with slug-like Kimberella grazing a green microbial mat and leaving scratch trails behind.
note: Museum case seen from above; the frame edge shows.

subject: Frond fossil, Mistaken Point
caption: A feathery Ediacaran frond pressed into the rock at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, about 565 million years old; a coin gives the scale.

subject: Burgess Shale quarry slope
caption: The scree slope below Walcott's quarry high in the Canadian Rockies today, where the Burgess Shale fossils of the Cambrian sea were found.
note: Present-day photo of the fossil site.

subject: End-Ordovician sea retreat
caption: Long-shelled nautiloids lie stranded on a drained sea floor as ice ages lowered the oceans at the end of the Ordovician.
note: An artist's interpretation of the end-Ordovician extinction; the scene is imagined, not based on one fossil site.

subject: Sacabambaspis
caption: Sacabambaspis, an armoured jawless fish of Ordovician seas, swims head-on toward the viewer.

subject: Waukesha biota
caption: Life on a Silurian sea floor in what is now Wisconsin: a horseshoe-crab-like arthropod, worms, small crustaceans and a looming nautiloid.
note: Small artist's name in the lower right corner.

subject: Guiyu
caption: Guiyu, one of the earliest bony fish, swims over a reef in a Silurian sea in what is now China.
note: Portrait format.

subject: Pterygotus
caption: Pterygotus, a giant sea scorpion with long grasping claws that hunted in Silurian and Devonian seas.
note: Drawn on a white background.

subject: Cooksonia
caption: Cooksonia, one of the first land plants, a few centimetres tall, rising from bare Silurian mud.
note: Small file (900 px). Simple 3D render.

subject: Silurian shore
caption: A calm Silurian sea with colourful reefs of corals and sea lilies, painted by Charles R. Knight.
note: Early 20th-century painting; the reef colours are imagined.

subject: Gooloogongia
caption: Gooloogongia, a large predatory lobe-finned fish of Devonian rivers in Australia.

subject: Jaekelopterus
caption: Jaekelopterus, the largest sea scorpion ever found, about 2.5 metres long, from Devonian waters in Germany.

subject: Devonian sea floor with Terataspis
caption: A museum diorama of a Devonian reef with the large spiny trilobite Terataspis among corals and sea lilies.

subject: Acanthostega
caption: Acanthostega, an early four-legged animal with gills and a fish-like tail that still lived in water.
note: Very wide cut-out on a white background.

subject: Arthropleura
caption: Arthropleura, a millipede relative over two metres long that crawled through Carboniferous forests.
note: Cut-out on a white background.

subject: Meganeura
caption: A model of Meganeura, a dragonfly-like insect with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres from the Carboniferous.
note: Museum model photographed on white.

subject: Carboniferous sea lilies
caption: Orange sea lilies sway in a museum diorama of a Carboniferous sea floor, with a fish painted in the background.
note: Colours in the diorama are imagined.

subject: Moschops
caption: Two Moschops, heavily built plant-eating relatives of mammals, from the Permian of South Africa.

subject: Sinophoneus
caption: A family of Sinophoneus, a big Permian relative of mammals from China, with a young one at the bottom.
credit: He who needs to be silenced
note: Dark background.

subject: Siberian Traps, Putorana Plateau
caption: The stepped lava cliffs of the Putorana Plateau in Siberia today, part of the Siberian Traps whose eruptions are blamed for the end-Permian mass extinction.
note: Present-day aerial photo; the lavas erupted about 252 million years ago.

subject: Saurosuchus and Hyperodapedon
caption: Saurosuchus, a large Triassic predator related to crocodiles, faces a herd of beaked Hyperodapedon in Argentina.

subject: Fallen conifers, Chinle Formation
caption: A painting of a Late Triassic river plain in Arizona strewn with fallen conifer logs, the trees that became the Petrified Forest.
note: Photo of a museum painting.

subject: Whale skeleton in the desert, Wadi Al-Hitan
caption: The skeleton of an Eocene whale weathering out of the desert floor at Wadi Al-Hitan, Egypt, where a sea lay 40 million years ago.

subject: Andrewsarchus
caption: Andrewsarchus, a large Eocene meat-eating mammal from Mongolia known mainly from a huge skull.
note: Only the skull is known, so the body is a guess.

subject: Paraceratherium herd
caption: A herd of Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal ever, browsing on an open plain in an early 20th-century painting.
note: Painted in the 1920s; the animals' proportions are dated.

subject: Hoplophoneus
caption: Hoplophoneus, a sabre-toothed cat-like hunter of Oligocene North America.
note: Cut-out on a white background.

subject: Batallones fauna
caption: Animals of the late Miocene Batallones fossil pits near Madrid, including sabre-toothed cats, a bear-dog and a mastodon.
note: Line-up on a white background.

subject: Paratethys sea
caption: A whale and a giant elephant relative meet on the shore of the Paratethys, a huge inland sea that covered eastern Europe in the Miocene.
note: Smaller file (1403 px).

subject: Kelenken
caption: Kelenken, a terror bird with the biggest skull of any known bird, feeds in Miocene Patagonia.

subject: Livyatan
caption: Livyatan, a sperm-whale relative with teeth up to 36 centimetres long that hunted in Miocene seas.
note: Cut-out on a white background.

subject: The young Earth under bombardment
caption: Meteors streak through a dark sky over glowing lava fields on the young Earth, in a NASA artist's view of the planet's violent first age.
credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab
note: An artist's impression; how much of the Hadean surface was molten, and when oceans first formed, is still debated (zircons hint at liquid water by 4.4 billion years ago). Very wide banner.

subject: Birth of the planets
caption: A young star wrapped in a glowing disc of gas and dust, the kind of disc in which Earth and the other planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
note: Shows another young star, not the Sun; a stand-in for the birth of the Solar System.

subject: Cratered lunar highlands
caption: Crater upon crater on the Moon's highlands, photographed from Apollo 17 in 1972; the Moon still keeps the scars of the bombardment that also struck the young Earth.
note: Present-day photo of the Moon, standing in for the battered surface of the Hadean Earth.

subject: Lava lake at dusk, Kīlauea
caption: A crusted lake of molten lava glows at dusk in Kīlauea's summit crater in Hawaii in 2021, a modern glimpse of the molten surfaces of the young Earth.
note: Present-day photo used as an analogue.

subject: Allende meteorite
caption: A slice of the Allende meteorite, whose pale grains are about 4.567 billion years old, among the first solids to form in the Solar System.
note: Museum photo with reflections; older than the Earth itself.

subject: Microbial mats, Grand Prismatic Spring
caption: Orange carpets of microbes spread from the steaming Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone today, a modern analogue of the microbial world of the Archean.
note: Present-day photo; the colours come from bacteria and other microbes living in the hot water.

subject: Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains
caption: Misty green hills of the Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains in South Africa today, built of some of the best-preserved rocks on Earth, 3.2 to 3.6 billion years old.
note: Present-day panorama (very wide).
imageDateLabel: Present day · rocks 3.2–3.6 billion years old

subject: Strelley Pool stromatolite
caption: Wavy layers in a slab from the Strelley Pool rocks of Western Australia, among the oldest widely accepted traces of life, about 3.4 billion years old.
note: Most scientists read these layers as microbial, but a non-living origin has been argued for some very old stromatolites.
imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 3.4 billion years ago

subject: Isua banded iron, Greenland
caption: Banded iron rock about 3.8 billion years old from the Isua belt of Greenland, one of the oldest sedimentary rocks on Earth.
note: A small museum label shows on the specimen.
imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 3.8 billion years ago

subject: Komatiite lava
caption: Needle-like 'spinifex' crystals in komatiite, an extremely hot lava that erupted often in the Archean but almost never since; Ontario, about 2.7 billion years old.
imageDateLabel: Lava erupted about 2.7 billion years ago

subject: Banded iron, Hamersley Range
caption: Red jasper, grey iron oxide and golden tiger-eye bands in a banded iron formation from the Hamersley Range, Western Australia, about 2.5 billion years old.
note: Close-up of a polished rock surface; the age straddles the Archean-Proterozoic boundary.
imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 2.5 billion years ago

subject: Microbial mats, Yellowstone
caption: Cracked, orange microbial mats around the Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone today, a modern analogue of the mats that carpeted shallow water through the long Proterozoic.
note: Present-day photo used as an analogue.

subject: Vishnu Schist, Grand Canyon
caption: Rafts drift beneath cliffs of Vishnu Schist in the inner Grand Canyon today, rock formed about 1.75 billion years ago when island arcs crashed into early North America.
note: Present-day photo.
imageDateLabel: Present day · rocks about 1.75 billion years old

subject: The Great Unconformity
caption: In the Grand Canyon, flat Cambrian sandstone sits directly on dark Proterozoic schist; over a billion years of Earth's record is missing at the join.
note: Present-day photo; deep shadows.

subject: Charnia
caption: Charnia, a frond-shaped Ediacaran organism that grew anchored to the deep sea floor about 570 to 555 million years ago.
note: Cut-out on a white background; the colours are imagined.

subject: Marjum biota, Utah
caption: A Cambrian sea floor in what is now Utah, with radiodont predators overhead, trilobites, sponges and sea lilies, about 500 million years ago.
note: Figure from a paper: small key numbers sit beside each animal.

subject: Astraspis
caption: Astraspis, one of the earliest armoured jawless fish, stirs up sand on an Ordovician sea floor.
note: Close to square, on a pale background.

subject: Anji glass-sponge reef
caption: A large trilobite-like arthropod crawls through a dark forest of glass sponges on an Ordovician sea floor in what is now China.
note: Small artist's mark in the lower left corner.

subject: Cabrières biota
caption: A crowded Early Ordovician sea floor in southern France, with algae, sponges, a large nautiloid and dozens of small animals, about 470 million years ago.
note: Wide format (1950 px).

subject: Nautiloids over a Late Ordovician sea floor
caption: Long straight-shelled nautiloids hunt among sea lilies and seaweed in a museum diorama of the Late Ordovician sea that covered Ohio.
note: Diorama colours are imagined.

subject: Isotelus trilobite
caption: The large trilobite Isotelus crawls past orange bryozoans in a museum diorama of the Late Ordovician sea floor of Ohio.

subject: Late Ordovician reef life
caption: Yellow sea lilies, corals, clams and a nautiloid's tentacles in a museum diorama of the Late Ordovician sea floor of Ohio.

subject: Rugose corals
caption: Horn-shaped rugose corals with their tentacles out, a coral group that first appeared in the Ordovician and died out at the end of the Permian.
note: 3D render on a black background; the colours are imagined.

subject: Endoceras
caption: Endoceras, a nautiloid with a straight shell that could reach several metres, one of the largest animals of Ordovician seas.
note: Cut-out on a white background.

subject: Nesonektris
caption: Nesonektris, a strange swimming vetulicolian, glides through shallow Cambrian water.
credit: He who needs to be silenced
note: What group vetulicolians belong to is still debated.

subject: Silurian reef
caption: A busy Silurian reef in a museum diorama: corals, sea lilies, snails, trilobites, a nautiloid and an early fish.
note: Diorama colours are imagined.

subject: Trilobite on a Silurian reef
caption: A trilobite rests on a coral head among sea lilies and bryozoans in a museum diorama of a Silurian reef.

subject: Sea scorpions in a Silurian lagoon
caption: Sea scorpions stalk through seaweed in a museum diorama of a shallow Silurian lagoon.

subject: Sea stacks of Gotland
caption: Limestone sea stacks on the coast of Gotland, Sweden, today; they are the remains of reefs that grew in a warm Silurian sea about 425 million years ago.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Niagara Falls
caption: Niagara Falls today; the hard ledge the water pours over is dolostone laid down on the floor of a shallow tropical Silurian sea.
note: Present-day photo; the falls themselves were cut after the last ice age.

subject: Dickinsonia
caption: A ribbed oval impression of Dickinsonia from South Australia; traces of cholesterol in such fossils suggest it was one of the earliest animals.

subject: Spriggina
caption: The small segmented Ediacaran fossil Spriggina, about 3 centimetres long, on a slab from the Ediacara Hills of South Australia.
note: What kind of animal Spriggina was is still uncertain.

subject: Devonian reef with trilobites
caption: Corals, sea lilies and spiny trilobites crowd a museum diorama of a Devonian reef in New York.

subject: Joggins Fossil Cliffs
caption: The Joggins Fossil Cliffs on the Bay of Fundy, Nova Scotia, today; their layers hold upright fossil trees and early reptiles of the Carboniferous coal forests.
note: Present-day photo; a very wide panorama.

subject: Gastornis
caption: Gastornis, a giant flightless bird, walks across open woodland in a 1917 drawing.
note: Gastornis lived from the late Paleocene into the Eocene. Black-and-white drawing; the bird's feathering is a guess.

subject: Paleocene badlands, Painted Canyon
caption: Badlands of Painted Canyon in North Dakota today, carved from river and swamp deposits laid down in the Paleocene, soon after the dinosaurs died out.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Paraceratherium skull
caption: The skull of Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal known, in the American Museum of Natural History.
note: Museum photo with reflections in the glass.

subject: Hyaenodon gigas
caption: Hyaenodon gigas, a large meat-eating mammal of the late Eocene in Asia, from a group unrelated to modern cats and dogs.
note: Cut-out on white with a 50 cm scale bar.

subject: Inostrancevia attacking Scutosaurus
caption: The sabre-toothed Inostrancevia brings down a Scutosaurus on a late Permian plain in Russia.
note: Shows a kill, with some blood.

subject: Barylambda
caption: Barylambda, a heavy, slow plant-eating mammal the size of a pony from the late Paleocene of North America.
note: Cut-out on a white background.

subject: Painted Canyon, Theodore Roosevelt National Park
caption: Badlands under towering clouds in Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, today; the layers are Paleocene muds and sands from rivers and swamp forests.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Paleocene petrified logs
caption: Petrified tree trunks weathering out of the badlands in Theodore Roosevelt National Park, remains of Paleocene swamp forests of redwood-like trees.

subject: Painted Canyon in spring
caption: Green grass and striped Paleocene layers in Painted Canyon, North Dakota, today.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Painted Hills, Oregon
caption: The banded Painted Hills of Oregon today, made of volcanic ash soils that weathered under a warm, wet climate around the Eocene-Oligocene boundary.
note: Present-day panorama (very wide). The layers span roughly 39 to 30 million years ago.

subject: Painted Hills with wildflowers
caption: Wildflowers in front of the red and gold Painted Hills of the John Day Fossil Beds, Oregon, today.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Hagerman horse
caption: A skeleton of the Hagerman horse, Equus simplicidens, one of the earliest members of the horse genus, from about 3.5 million years ago in Idaho.
note: Museum photo.

subject: Late Miocene Oregon
caption: Horses, camels and other grazers cross a grassland in late Miocene Oregon as a volcanic ash cloud rolls in, in a mural for the John Day Fossil Beds.
note: Public-domain mural painted for a US federal agency; very wide.

subject: Ischigualasto, Valley of the Moon
caption: The grey badlands of Ischigualasto in Argentina today, Late Triassic rocks that hold some of the oldest dinosaurs, such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus.
note: Present-day panorama.

subject: Eryops
caption: Eryops, a big early Permian amphibian, lies among ferns and horsetails in a museum diorama of a swampy forest floor.

subject: Dimetrodon in a forest diorama
caption: A model Dimetrodon, a sail-backed early Permian predator related to mammals, in a museum diorama of a fern forest.

subject: Mississippian sea lilies
caption: Sea lilies with arms like lace in a museum diorama of an early Carboniferous sea floor, when crinoids formed vast meadows.

subject: Late Carboniferous sea
caption: Fish, sponges, a coiled nautiloid and shells on a late Carboniferous sea floor, in a museum diorama.
note: Diorama colours are imagined.

subject: Fossil tree standing in the cliff, Joggins
caption: A fossil scale-tree trunk still standing upright where it grew, buried in the Carboniferous cliffs of Joggins, Nova Scotia; a hammer gives scale.

subject: Postosuchus, Coelophysis and Placerias
caption: The big predator Postosuchus, small Coelophysis dinosaurs and a herd of tusked Placerias share a Late Triassic river plain in what is now the American Southwest.

subject: Burgess Shale sea floor
caption: Worms, the lobopodian Aysheaia, a trilobite and the lace crab Marrella on the sea floor in a museum diorama of the Burgess Shale.
note: Older museum diorama; some animals are shown as they were understood in past decades.

subject: Fortiforceps and Sklerolibyon
caption: Two early Cambrian arthropods with grasping head claws, Fortiforceps and Sklerolibyon, in a sea in what is now southern China.

subject: Dinictis and Protoceras
caption: The cat-like hunter Dinictis watches a group of horned Protoceras in an Oligocene landscape painted by Charles R. Knight in 1904.
note: Painted in 1904; details are dated.

subject: Flysch cliffs near Zumaia
caption: Tilted layers of deep-sea rock in the cliffs near Zumaia, Spain, today; this coast holds the world reference points for two of the Paleocene's ages.
note: Present-day photo. The Zumaia flysch spans the Late Cretaceous to the Eocene; not every layer in view is Paleocene.

subject: Ankalagon
caption: Ankalagon, a wolf-sized meat-eating mammal from the early Paleocene of New Mexico, shown as a female and a larger male.
note: Cut-out with labels and a scale bar.

subject: Alcidedorbignya
caption: Alcidedorbignya, a small early Paleocene mammal from Bolivia, one of the first of the plant-eating pantodonts.
note: Cut-out on white with a 5 cm scale bar.

subject: Wilpena Pound
caption: Sunset lights the quartzite walls of Wilpena Pound in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia today; rock layers in these ranges hold the Ediacaran fossils and gave the period its name.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Ounianga lakes from space
caption: The blue Ounianga lakes in the Sahara of Chad seen from the International Space Station, leftovers of the much larger lakes of the 'Green Sahara' in the early Holocene.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Lake Yoa
caption: Lake Yoa in the Chad desert today; its layered mud records how the green Sahara of the early Holocene dried into desert over thousands of years.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Göbekli Tepe
caption: Stone pillars at Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, raised about 11,000 years ago, at the very start of the Holocene, by people who had not yet begun farming.
note: Excavation photo; scaffolding and fences are visible.

subject: Rock engraving of an extinct buffalo
caption: A rock engraving of a giant buffalo from Tin Taghirt in the Algerian Sahara, carved when the region was green grassland in the early Holocene.
note: The age of Saharan rock engravings is hard to pin down; estimates for this style range widely.

subject: Cattle herders in Saharan rock art
caption: People and cattle painted on a rock shelter in the Sahara, a record of the herders who lived there when it was greener, several thousand years ago.
note: Exact site and date of the painting are not given on the file page.

subject: Dodo
caption: A dodo skeleton; this flightless pigeon of Mauritius was wiped out by the late 1600s, within a century of people arriving.
note: Museum photo.

subject: Pliocene grazers of East Africa
caption: Giraffes, antelopes, pigs, a three-toed horse and a rhino from the Pliocene of East Africa, drawn by Mauricio Antón.
note: Black-and-white line-up on a grid.

subject: Pliocene North America
caption: Rhinos wallow and mastodons graze by a lake in Charles R. Knight's mural of Pliocene North America.
note: Early 20th-century painting; animals and dating are old interpretations. Very wide.

subject: Thalassocnus
caption: Thalassocnus, a ground sloth that waded into the sea to graze on seagrass along the desert coast of Peru.
note: Cut-out on white. Thalassocnus species lived from the late Miocene into the Pliocene.

subject: Deinotherium
caption: Deinotherium, a huge elephant relative with tusks curving down from its lower jaw, beside a human silhouette for scale.
note: Cut-out on white. Deinotherium lived from the Miocene into the Pleistocene.

subject: Blue Mesa, Petrified Forest
caption: Striped badlands and fallen stone logs at Blue Mesa in Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, today; the logs are conifers that grew about 220 million years ago.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: El Capitan, a Permian reef
caption: Snow on El Capitan in the Guadalupe Mountains of Texas today; the cliff is part of a reef that ringed a Permian sea about 260 million years ago.
note: Present-day photo.

subject: Lemurosaurus
caption: Lemurosaurus, a small late Permian relative of mammals from South Africa.
note: Cut-out on white with a 10 cm scale bar.

subject: Old Red Sandstone
caption: Red sandstone and pebble beds in the sea cliffs at Auchmithie, Scotland, today, laid down by rivers on a dry Devonian continent.
note: A person at the far right gives scale.

subject: Archaeotherium
caption: Two Archaeotherium, big pig-like 'hell pigs' of Oligocene North America, root at a carcass in a drawing by R. Bruce Horsfall.
note: Early 20th-century black-and-white drawing; entelodonts were not true pigs.

subject: Kimberella fossil
caption: A fossil of Kimberella from the White Sea coast of Russia, about 555 million years old; many scientists think it was an early mollusc-like animal.
note: Kimberella's place among animals is still debated.

subject: Gilboa tree stump
caption: The fossil base of an Eospermatopteris tree from Gilboa, New York, one of the trees of the first forests on Earth, about 385 million years ago.
note: Museum photo of a rock stump; portrait format.

subject: Ediacaran sea floor
caption: Pink and orange fronds, quilted discs and other soft Ediacaran organisms cover the sea floor in a diorama at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History.
note: Colours are imagined; how these organisms lived is still debated.

subject: Kimberella
caption: Kimberella, a soft-bodied Ediacaran animal, creeps across a green microbial mat that it may have grazed.
note: 3D render; the body shape follows one interpretation of the fossils.

subject: Camp dels Ninots crater lake
caption: Deer, tapirs and birds around a volcanic crater lake in a Pliocene forest in Catalonia, Spain, about 3 million years ago, painted by Mauricio Antón.
note: Wide format.

subject: Ardi
caption: A cast of 'Ardi', the 4.4-million-year-old skeleton of Ardipithecus ramidus from Ethiopia, an early member of the human line who walked upright but also climbed trees.
note: Museum photo of a cast; how Ardipithecus is related to later hominins is debated.

subject: Scale-tree stump
caption: The scaly stump of a Lepidodendron tree and a large mayfly-like insect in a museum diorama of a late Carboniferous coal-swamp floor.

subject: Thylacine
caption: A thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, photographed at Hobart Zoo in 1928; the last known one died there in 1936.
note: Historical black-and-white photo with a dark border.

subject: Hyracodon
caption: Two Hyracodon, slender, long-legged hornless rhinos of the Oligocene plains, squabble in a 1912 drawing by R. Bruce Horsfall.
note: Early 20th-century black-and-white drawing; the artist's signature shows in the corner.

subject: Mesohippus
caption: A small herd of Mesohippus, three-toed horses the size of a large dog, in an Oligocene woodland drawn by R. Bruce Horsfall in 1913.
note: Early 20th-century drawing; the spotted coat is the artist's guess.

subject: Isthmus of Panama
caption: The Isthmus of Panama from space today; when this land bridge closed in the Pliocene, animals crossed between the Americas and ocean currents changed.
credit: Jeff Schmaltz, MODIS Rapid Response Team, NASA
note: Present-day satellite image. Most scientists date the full closure to about 3 million years ago, but some argue for a much earlier link.

subject: Kanapoi, Kenya
caption: Dry country near Lake Turkana in northern Kenya seen from space; Kanapoi's 4.2-million-year-old rocks yielded Australopithecus anamensis, the earliest known Australopithecus.
note: Present-day astronaut photo; the fossil site itself is too small to pick out.

subject: Painted Canyon under cloud
caption: Grassy slopes and banded buttes of Paleocene rock stretch to the horizon in Painted Canyon, North Dakota, today.
note: Present-day photo; flat light.

subject: Taeniolabis
caption: The head of Taeniolabis, a beaver-sized multituberculate, one of the largest mammals of the early Paleocene, drawn by R. Bruce Horsfall.
note: Early 20th-century drawing of the head only.

subject: Snowball Earth
caption: An artist's view of the Earth almost entirely frozen over, as it was during the great Cryogenian glaciations.
note: Painted for the earlier Huronian glaciation about 2.4 billion years ago; the outlines of the land are not a reconstruction.

subject: The end of a Snowball Earth
caption: At Enorama Creek in South Australia, pale limestone laid down as the last Snowball Earth melted sits on top of the glacial rocks; this layer marks the start of the Ediacaran, about 635 million years ago.
imageDateLabel: Rock formed about 635 million years ago

subject: An acritarch
caption: A spiny acritarch, a microscopic fossil less than a millimetre across, from the Weng'an rocks of southern China; acritarchs are the walls of single cells, many probably algae, whose true nature is unknown.

note: Scanning electron microscope image of Mengeosphaera.

subject: Grypania
caption: Coiled ribbons of Grypania in iron-rich rock from Michigan, among the oldest fossils big enough to see with the naked eye and probably early algae.
note: The rock is dated to either about 1.87 or 2.1 billion years ago; scientists disagree.

caption: During the Cryogenian glaciations ice spread across much of Earth. Its extent remains uncertain.
subject: Snowball Earth Globe

caption: Hallucigenia sparsa had seven pairs of defensive spines and soft legs. Burgess Shale fossils show an animal only a few centimetres long.
subject: Hallucigenia On Sponge

caption: Opabinia was a small animal with five eyes, a long grasping trunk and swimming flaps.
subject: Opabinia Seafloor

caption: Early Ordovician Fezouata fossils record a diverse marine fauna, including filter-feeding radiodonts.
subject: Fezouata Biota Scene
Devonian Shallows
caption: Lobe-finned fish lived in watery habitats during the Late Devonian, about 375 million years ago.

subject: Tiktaalik Shallows
caption: Tiktaalik, a fossil fish from about 375 million years ago, had a broad head, a neck and sturdy fins with rays.

subject: Acanthostega Water
caption: Acanthostega was a largely aquatic early tetrapod. Fossils show limbs with digits and a fish-like tail.

subject: Ichthyostega Water
caption: The robust skeleton and limbs of Ichthyostega are known from fossils; exactly how it moved on land is still debated.

subject: Fin Limb Comparison
caption: An illustrative comparison of a Tiktaalik-like fin and an Acanthostega-like limb. The generated skeletons are schematic, not anatomically exact or to scale; Acanthostega fossils show eight digits on the forelimb.

subject: Devonian Trackway
caption: Devonian traces in Poland record early trackways, although the makers of some tracks are debated.

subject: Dunkleosteus terrelli
caption: Dunkleosteus terrelli was an armoured fish of the Late Devonian. Fossils preserve the bony head armour and cutting jaw plates; its colour, fins, body shape and the surrounding sea are an artist’s interpretation. Its full size remains debated.

subject: Hyneria in a Devonian river
caption: Hyneria lindae was a large predatory lobe-finned fish that lived in Late Devonian waters of what is now Pennsylvania.

subject: Gooloogongia
caption: Gooloogongia loomesi was a lobe-finned fish known from Late Devonian fossils at Canowindra in Australia.

subject: Jaekelopterus
caption: Jaekelopterus rhenaniae was a large aquatic arthropod from the Early Devonian of what is now Germany. Fossils preserve parts including its claws.

subject: An early tetrapod at the water’s edge
caption: An Ichthyostega-like tetrapod at a shoreline around 365 million years ago. How it moved on land and how often it left the water are uncertain; the transition happened over many generations.

size.name: Ichthyostega-like tetrapod
size.note: The scene is a reconstruction; fossil individuals varied in size.

subject: Early Earth Lava
caption: Ancient zircon crystals suggest that solid crust and liquid water existed by about 4.4 billion years ago.

subject: Moon Forming Impact
caption: A possible Moon-forming impact. One leading explanation is that a large body struck the young Earth and debris gathered to form the Moon; the details remain uncertain.

subject: Early Earth Dusk
caption: Ancient crystals point to liquid water on the Hadean Earth; the shape of its coastlines and appearance of the sky are unknown.

subject: Planets Before Impact
caption: In the giant-impact hypothesis, a body often called Theia struck the early Earth; its exact appearance and orbit are unknown.

subject: Young Solar Disc
caption: The planets formed from a disc of gas and dust around the young Sun; the detailed appearance of the disc is unknown.

subject: Young Moon Highlands
caption: Lunar samples show that an early molten Moon cooled to form a light-coloured crust.

subject: Hadean Crater Lava
caption: Volcanism shaped the early Earth, but its particular landscapes are not known.

subject: Young Moon Impact
caption: The Moon’s ancient cratered surface preserves evidence of collisions early in solar system history.

subject: Early Earth Seafloor
caption: Ancient zircon chemistry suggests liquid water existed on the young Earth; the location and appearance of its earliest seafloor are unknown.

subject: A shallow Archean lagoon
caption: Layered rocks in the Pilbara preserve evidence of microbial mats and stromatolites about 3.4 billion years ago.

subject: An Archean volcanic coast
caption: Ancient volcanic rocks record eruptions beside Archean oceans.

subject: Microbial mats along a river
caption: Fossil evidence indicates microbial mats grew on river sediments about 3.22 billion years ago in what is now South Africa.

subject: The Archean Earth from space
caption: The Archean Earth had oceans and land; their arrangement and the presence of atmospheric haze are uncertain.

subject: Underwater volcanic eruption
caption: Rounded pillow lavas in Archean rocks record eruptions beneath water.

subject: A seafloor hydrothermal vent
caption: Hydrothermal vents release hot, mineral-rich fluids into the ocean. Whether microbes inhabited a particular ancient vent is uncertain.

subject: Archean hot springs
caption: Rocks in the Pilbara preserve evidence interpreted as hot-spring deposits about 3.48 billion years old, with possible microbial traces.

subject: An Archean glacial shore
caption: Deposits in southern Africa suggest glaciation about 2.9 billion years ago; the evidence does not show that the whole planet froze.

subject: An impact in an Archean ocean
caption: Layers of impact debris record ancient impacts during the Archean.

subject: A storm over an Archean river
caption: Fossil evidence indicates microbial mats grew on river sediments about 3.22 billion years ago in what is now South Africa.

subject: An iron-rich sea
caption: Ancient banded iron formations record the deposition of iron-rich minerals in early seas.

subject: A microbial shore during the Great Oxidation
caption: Microbial communities lived in shallow water as oxygen began to accumulate in the atmosphere over a long, uneven interval.

subject: Ice at an ancient coast
caption: Glacial deposits record ice ages in the early Paleoproterozoic; the extent of ice remains uncertain.

subject: A possible Francevillian seafloor
caption: Lobed structures in rocks from Gabon have been interpreted as large early life, but their origin and biological identity remain debated.

subject: The Vredefort impact
caption: Shocked and melted rocks record a giant impact at Vredefort in what is now South Africa about 2.02 billion years ago.

subject: The Gunflint microbial shallows
caption: Gunflint rocks preserve microbial fossils and iron-rich stromatolitic structures from an ancient sea.

subject: Continents collide
caption: Ancient mountain belts record continental collisions during the assembly of landmasses sometimes grouped as Columbia or Nuna.

subject: A microscopic view of early life
caption: The magnified circle shows simple filaments inspired by microscopic fossils from North China, interpreted as early multicellular eukaryotes.

subject: Microscopic life in the Roper sea
caption: A magnified view of microscopic life inspired by fossils from the Roper Group of Australia. Living colours, internal features and relative sizes are not known.

subject: A dry Belt Basin shore
caption: Mud cracks and other sedimentary features in Belt rocks record ancient shallow-water environments.

subject: The Moon over an ancient shore
caption: Rhythmic layers in ancient rocks provide estimates of the Earth–Moon system at this time. The Moon was closer than today.

subject: Lava in the Midcontinent Rift
caption: Basalt flows record volcanism during the formation of North America’s Midcontinent Rift.

subject: A lake in the rift
caption: Sediments of the Nonesuch Formation record an ancient lake within the rift.

subject: Bangiomorpha under magnification
caption: A magnified view of Bangiomorpha, a microscopic filamentous red alga. Its living colour and exact appearance are uncertain.

subject: Rodinia coming together
caption: Continental blocks were assembling into Rodinia; their arrangement and coastlines remain uncertain.

subject: A conceptual early eukaryotic cell
caption: A magnified conceptual cutaway showing a nucleus and mitochondrion-like structures in a eukaryotic cell. Internal details are inferred from cell biology, not observed in a particular Mesoproterozoic fossil.

subject: A tiny green alga
caption: Proterocladus fossils preserve tiny branched, multicellular forms measured in millimetres. This view is magnified; exact proportions and living colours are uncertain.

subject: Inside a microbial reef
caption: Textures in microbial reefs about 890 million years old have been proposed as sponge fossils, but that interpretation is disputed.

subject: A world of microscopic scales
caption: Fossil mineral scales show that some Tonian microorganisms made intricate coverings. This view is magnified; their whole living forms remain uncertain.

subject: A sheltered Tonian lagoon
caption: Fossils record microscopic life in late Tonian waters, including sheltered coastal environments.

subject: Vase-shaped microscopic life
caption: Vase-shaped microfossils are interpreted as the tiny outer coverings of amoeba-like cells. Their living soft parts are uncertain; this view is magnified.

subject: Rodinia begins to pull apart
caption: Geological evidence records the stretching and breakup of Rodinia. The arrangement of its landmasses remains uncertain.

subject: A late Tonian volcanic coast
caption: Volcanic rocks record major eruptions near the end of the Tonian. The Sturtian glaciation followed near the beginning of the Cryogenian.

subject: A coast before the great freeze
caption: The Sturtian glaciation began near the start of the Cryogenian, after the Tonian Period.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Ancient zircon crystals suggest liquid water and a solid crust existed by about 4.3 billion years ago. The extent and arrangement of early land are unknown.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Early continental blocks grew and collided during the Paleoproterozoic. Their arrangement and coastlines remain uncertain.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Continental blocks began to separate during Rodinia’s breakup. Their exact positions and coastlines remain uncertain.

subject: A view from the mountains
caption: Ancient zircon crystals suggest that Earth had a solid crust and liquid water by about 4.3 billion years ago. The extent and position of early land are unknown.

subject: A view from the mountains
caption: Rivers crossed Archean land, and fossil evidence shows microbial mats on river sediments about 3.22 billion years ago.

subject: A view from the mountains
caption: Glacial deposits record ice ages in the early Paleoproterozoic. The total extent of ice remains uncertain.

subject: A view from the mountains
caption: The Nonesuch Formation preserves sediments from an ancient lake within North America’s Midcontinent Rift.

subject: A view from the mountains
caption: Geological records show continental stretching and rifting during the breakup of Rodinia. The positions of its landmasses remain uncertain.

subject: Earth during the Sturtian
caption: Glacial deposits show ice reached low latitudes during the Sturtian. Whether sea ice covered the entire ocean remains debated.

subject: Above the Sturtian ice
caption: Glaciers reached low-latitude coasts during the Sturtian glaciation; the extent of sea ice remains uncertain.

subject: Ice reaches the coast
caption: Dated glacial deposits show that ice reached sea level near the tropics during the Sturtian glaciation.

subject: A possible refuge beneath the ice
caption: Microbes and algae survived the glaciations. Water beneath ice is one possible refuge, although the habitats and amount of light are uncertain.

subject: The Sturtian thaw
caption: The Sturtian glaciation ended around 660 million years ago, leaving evidence of a major transition from glacial conditions.

subject: The interval between glaciations
caption: A nonglacial interval separated the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations. Microbial life persisted through this period.

subject: The Marinoan glaciation
caption: The Marinoan was the second major Cryogenian glaciation. Its onset remains less securely dated than its end.

subject: The final thaw
caption: Carbonate layers above glacial deposits mark a major environmental transition at the end of the Marinoan glaciation.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Continental blocks were coming together to form Gondwana. Their exact positions and coastlines remain uncertain.

subject: Above the Gaskiers coast
caption: Glacial deposits in what is now Newfoundland record the Gaskiers ice age. The extent of ice beyond the regions with known deposits is uncertain.

subject: The microscopic world of Weng’an
caption: The Weng’an rocks of South China preserve tiny spheres with clusters of cells. Some resemble embryos, but their biological identity is disputed. This is a magnified view.

subject: A deep seafloor at Mistaken Point
caption: Frond-shaped rangeomorphs stood above the deep seafloor, while spindle-shaped Fractofusus lay along it. Beds of volcanic ash helped preserve these communities.

subject: Dickinsonia on a microbial mat
caption: Fossils preserve Dickinsonia’s flat, ribbed body. Lipids preserved with some specimens support its identification as one of the earliest known animals.

subject: Kimberella and its feeding traces
caption: Fan-shaped scratches found near Kimberella fossils suggest it scraped food from the seafloor. Chemical evidence also points to a diet that included algae and bacteria.

subject: A threefold body plan
caption: Three curving ridges distinguish Tribrachidium. Simulations of water flowing over its body suggest it may have captured suspended food.

subject: Small skeletons build a reef
caption: Reefs in Namibia’s Nama Group preserve small Cloudina tubes and cup-shaped Namacalathus. Many small skeletons helped build much larger reef structures.

subject: The last Ediacaran seas
caption: Fossils from Jiangchuan in what is now Yunnan preserve Ediacaran forms alongside bilaterian body fossils and traces of movement, shortly before the Cambrian.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Gondwana covered much of the Southern Hemisphere while Laurentia lay near the equator. The positions and coastlines of ancient continents are approximate.

subject: Above the Chengjiang delta
caption: Sediments in what is now Yunnan suggest the Chengjiang community lived in a delta where rivers delivered sediment to the sea.
Treptichnus pedum consists of linked probing burrows. Fossil traces preserve patterns of activity, but the identity of the animal that made them is uncertain.
Halkieria had a covering of small scales and a shell at each end.

size.name: Halkieria
size.note: Approximate; individuals varied.

subject: An archaeocyath reef
caption: Cup-shaped archaeocyath sponges and calcifying microbes built some of the earliest animal reefs. Their skeletons created shelter for other seafloor life.
Fish-like animals, trilobites and sponges are known from early Cambrian Chengjiang fossils.
Fossils of Kerygmachela from the early Cambrian Sirius Passet preserve lateral flaps, frontal appendages and a tail spine; colours and behaviour are uncertain.

size.name: Kerygmachela
size.note: Fossils preserve the body; total length is uncertain.

size.name: Haikouichthys
size.note: Approximate; fossil individuals vary.

size.name: Anomalocaris canadensis

subject: A late Cambrian shelf
caption: Trilobite fossils help date the early Furongian. Carbon isotope changes in marine rocks record a disruption to the carbon cycle around this time.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Gondwana extended toward the south pole while the Iapetus Ocean separated other continents. The positions and coastlines are approximate.

subject: Above the Taconic coast
caption: Collisions along Laurentia’s eastern margin raised mountains during the Taconic orogeny, an early chapter in Appalachian mountain building.
Early Ordovician Fezouata fossils record a diverse marine fauna, including filter-feeding radiodonts.

caption: Aegirocassis was an Early Ordovician filter-feeding radiodont that grew more than two metres long, after the Cambrian.

size.name: Aegirocassis

subject: Early plants on land
caption: Microscopic spores provide evidence for small early land plants. Their exact appearance is uncertain. The inset shows a magnified cluster of four spores.

subject: Life on a shallow Ordovician shelf
caption: Diversification in Ordovician seas produced communities rich in brachiopods, bryozoans, crinoids and corals. Straight-shelled cephalopods also lived in these seas.

subject: Ice reaches Gondwana’s coast
caption: Glacial deposits record ice reaching the margins of Gondwana during the Hirnantian. The advance and retreat of ice also affected sea levels far from the ice sheets.

subject: Survivors on the late Ordovician shelf
caption: The end-Ordovician extinction unfolded in two pulses. The organisms that survived and the severity of losses varied by habitat. The causes of each pulse remain debated.
Geologists in hard hats on the tilted rock layers at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, the world reference point for the start of the Cambrian.
Small shelly fossils from the earliest Cambrian of Shaanxi, China, seen under an electron microscope: tiny tubes and plates less than a millimetre long.
A fossil Anomalocaris eye preserved in pyrite, showing its honeycomb of tiny lenses.
Olenellus, an early Cambrian trilobite from Vermont, on display in the National Museum of Natural History, Paris.
note: Olenellus lived somewhat after the very first trilobites.

caption: The Maotianshan Shale near Chengjiang, Yunnan, where the Chengjiang fossils were found, now protected inside a museum building.
Retifacies, an arthropod from Chengjiang with a net-patterned armour, preserved in yellow mudstone.
A slab with Haikouichthys fossils, outlined and labelled in ink, at the Paleozoological Museum of China in Beijing.
A Burgess Shale fossil of Wiwaxia corrugata, an oval animal covered in overlapping scales with two rows of spines.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Gondwana covered much of the south while the Iapetus Ocean narrowed between Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia. The positions and coastlines are approximate.

subject: From a Caledonian mountaintop
caption: Continental collisions raised the Caledonian mountains as the Iapetus Ocean closed. Parts of the range survive in Scotland, Norway and Greenland.

subject: Early jawed fish in Chongqing
caption: The small armoured Xiushanosteus and the early shark relative Shenacanthus are known from unusually complete fossils in the same fossil beds in Chongqing, China.

size.name: Xiushanosteus
size.note: Shenacanthus measures about 2.2 cm from snout to anal fin in the fossil

subject: Cooksonia on wet ground
caption: Cooksonia stood only a few centimetres tall. Fossils preserve simple forked stems and spore capsules at their tips.

subject: Sollasina on the Herefordshire seabed
caption: Sollasina was a small relative of sea cucumbers. Its Herefordshire fossil preserves fleshy tube feet, which probably helped it move and feed.

size.name: Sollasina
size.note: About 3 cm across the fossil, including tube feet

subject: Gotland’s living reef
caption: Stromatoporoid sponges and ancient corals built reefs in the Silurian sea. Reef limestone survives in the cliffs and sea stacks of Gotland, Sweden.

subject: A bony fish in the Yunnan sea
caption: Guiyu was an early bony fish from what is now Yunnan, China. Its closely packed, diamond-shaped scales and parts of its bony armour are preserved in the fossil.

size.name: Guiyu
size.note: Estimated from a fossil missing the tail fin

subject: Sea scorpions in the shallows
caption: Eurypterus swam with broad paddles on its rear pair of limbs. Fossils from New York preserve the paddles, segmented body and straight tail spine.

size.name: Eurypterus remipes
size.note: Measured specimen PRI 70770

subject: Earth from space
caption: Laurussia lay near the equator and Gondwana stretched far to the south. Shallow seas covered parts of the continental margins.

subject: Above the Old Red Sandstone rivers
caption: Rivers in what is now eastern Scotland deposited red sand and gravel. Those deposits are visible today in cliffs around Arbroath and Auchmithie.

subject: Rhynie hot-spring wetland
caption: Small plants such as Rhynia and Asteroxylon grew in a wetland around hot springs. Silica from the spring water preserved parts of this ecosystem in the Rhynie chert.

subject: Inside the Gilboa forest
caption: Fossil stumps and an attached crown show how Wattieza grew. Tall trunks carried crowns of forked branches above the damp forest floor.

subject: Along the Gogo barrier reef
caption: Fossils from the Gogo reef complex in Western Australia include armoured fish such as Mcnamaraspis and lobe-finned fish such as Gogonasus.

size.name: Mcnamaraspis
size.note: Measured fossil head

subject: A fish carrying young
caption: A Materpiscis fossil from Gogo preserves an embryo and its umbilical cord. It is direct evidence that some Devonian armoured fish gave birth to live young.

subject: A reef before the Kellwasser crisis
caption: Reef-building sponges and corals supported diverse seafloor communities before the Kellwasser extinction. This coastal reef sets the scene for the next picture.

subject: A reef after the Kellwasser crisis
caption: A reduced reef community after the Kellwasser extinction pulse. Trace fossils and sediment chemistry indicate low and variable oxygen in some seas.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Gondwana and Laurussia were joining to form Pangaea. Shallow seas covered parts of the continental margins, and ice reached parts of southern Gondwana.

subject: From a Variscan mountaintop
caption: The collision that brought Pangaea together raised the Variscan mountains. At low latitudes, river basins between uplands supported wetlands where peat accumulated.

subject: A sea-lily meadow
caption: Stalked sea lilies and blastoids filtered food from currents above the seafloor. Their fossils are abundant in the Burlington Limestone in what is now Iowa.

subject: Arthropleura on a sandy riverbank
caption: A fossil from Howick in northern England preserves part of the broad, segmented armour of an unusually large Arthropleura. The sediments and plant remains indicate a relatively open coastal environment.

size.name: Arthropleura
size.note: Estimated from the partial Howick fossil

subject: At the edge of Gondwana’s ice
caption: Sediments in western Argentina record repeated Carboniferous advances and retreats of ice. Rock fragments dropped from floating ice are one clue that glaciers reached this region.

subject: Inside the Joggins coal forest
caption: The small early reptile Hylonomus lived among tall scale trees. At Joggins, Nova Scotia, bones of Hylonomus were found inside the remains of upright trees.

size.name: Hylonomus
size.note: Approximate size of the Joggins reptile

subject: The Tully monster in Mazon Creek waters
caption: Tullimonstrum had eyes on a crossbar and a long proboscis tipped with a small grasping mouth. Fossils from Illinois preserve both features. Its place on the animal family tree remains debated.

size.name: Tullimonstrum
size.note: Range estimated from fossil specimens

subject: Meganeura over a forest pool
caption: Meganeura was a giant griffinfly with four veined wings. Fossils from the coal basin at Commentry, France, preserve its wing shapes.

size.name: Meganeura
size.note: Estimate from the Commentry fossil

subject: Earth from space
caption: Pangaea stretched from north to south around an arm of the Tethys Ocean. Panthalassa covered much of the rest of Earth.

subject: From a young Ural ridge
caption: Continental collision raised the Urals and folded rocks along the edge of Baltica. Erosion carried sediment from the growing mountains into the basin below.

subject: Two sail-backed animals at a Texas pool
caption: Dimetrodon, a predator, and Edaphosaurus, a plant eater, were early relatives of mammals. Fossils from the Texas red beds preserve the tall spines that supported their sails.

size.name: Dimetrodon
size.note: Approximate adult size. Length varies by species.

subject: Mesosaurs in the Mangrullo basin
caption: Long-snouted mesosaurs lived in a basin in what is now Uruguay. The basin gradually became more isolated from the open sea, and the salinity varied as water evaporated.

size.note: Typical length estimated from fossil specimens

subject: Tracks across the Coconino dunes
caption: Footprints crossed windblown sand in what is now Arizona. Layers of that sand became the Coconino Sandstone. The tracks preserve toe marks, but the animal that made them is uncertain.

subject: Helicoprion in the Phosphoria Sea
caption: CT scans of a fossil from Idaho show how the tooth spiral sat inside the lower jaw. Most of the animal’s body is unknown from fossils.

subject: Earth from space

subject: Above a Chinle river plain
caption: Seasonal rivers crossed the Late Triassic lowlands of what is now the American Southwest. The Chinle Formation preserves floodplain sediments and fossil conifer wood.

subject: Earth from space
caption: Pangaea was breaking apart. The young Atlantic opened between the continental blocks, and shallow seas flooded parts of their margins.

subject: Above a Morrison floodplain
caption: River channels and floodplains left layers of sediment across western North America. These rocks make up much of the Morrison Formation, which preserves many Late Jurassic dinosaurs.

A sparsely vegetated Early Triassic river plain after the extinction. Forest loss and erosion are recorded in rocks, but the landscape varied and some plants survived.

Lystrosaurus, a beaked and tusked plant-eating relative of mammals, on an Early Triassic river plain. Several species survived the extinction; their sizes varied and their life appearance is uncertain.

size.name: Lystrosaurus
size.note: Different published estimates; not a measured range.

caption: Cartorhynchus was a short-snouted marine reptile related to ichthyosaurs. The known fossil was probably a juvenile; its tail is incompletely known.

size.name: Cartorhynchus
size.note: Tail estimated; specimen was probably juvenile.

caption: Teleocrater was a long-necked four-legged predator from Middle Triassic Tanzania, related to dinosaurs but not itself a dinosaur. Its skull, hands, feet and tail are incompletely known.

size.name: Teleocrater
size.note: Estimates; measurements vary by individual.

caption: Asilisaurus, a four-legged dinosaur relative from Middle Triassic Tanzania. It was not itself a dinosaur; its skin and colouring are unknown.

size.name: Asilisaurus
size.note: Estimates; measurements vary by individual.

subject: Early dinosaurs in Ischigualasto
caption: Fossils from the Ischigualasto Formation in Argentina include the lightly built Eoraptor and the larger predatory Herrerasaurus.

size.name: Eoraptor

subject: Plateosaurus in a river basin
caption: Late Triassic Plateosaurus was a long-necked early sauropodomorph. Its fossils are abundant at some Late Triassic sites in central Europe.

size.name: Plateosaurus
size.note: Estimated adult length; specimens vary

subject: An ichthyosaur and ammonite in a Jurassic sea
caption: Stenopterygius swam in Early Jurassic seas. Fossils preserve its streamlined body, just as ammonite shells preserve the shape of a very different swimmer.

size.name: Stenopterygius
size.note: Estimated total length

subject: Sauropods on the Morrison floodplain
caption: Long-necked sauropods and plated stegosaurs are known from the Morrison rocks of western North America. Diplodocus carried a very long tail, while Brachiosaurus stood higher at the shoulders.

size.name: Diplodocus
size.note: Estimated total length

subject: An early bird at a Jurassic lagoon
caption: Bavarian limestone preserves Archaeopteryx, an early bird with feathers, a long bony tail and teeth. Pterosaurs such as Rhamphorhynchus flew on membranes supported by an elongated finger.

size.name: Archaeopteryx
size.note: Estimated total length

caption: A cast of the Asilisaurus skeleton, rebuilt from at least 14 individuals found together in one Tanzanian bone bed, at the Field Museum in Chicago.
Two Plateosaurus skeletons dug from the clay pit at Trossingen, Germany, on display at the University of Tübingen.
note: Old mounts: the right-hand skeleton is posed on all fours, but Plateosaurus is now generally seen as walking on its hind legs. The species was then called P. engelhardti; the Trossingen animals are now P. trossingensis.

caption: A three-toed Eubrontes footprint from Early Jurassic rocks at Rocky Hill, Connecticut, left by a large meat-eating dinosaur.
note: No bones have been found with these tracks, so the exact maker is unknown.

caption: A fossil of Anchiornis from Liaoning with long feathers fanning out from its arms and legs.
A replica of the London specimen of Archaeopteryx, the first skeleton found (1861), with feather impressions on the wings and the long bony tail.
note: This is a cast at the Karlsruhe natural history museum; the original is in the Natural History Museum, London.

caption: A mounted skeleton of Lystrosaurus murrayi in the Natural History Museum in Paris.
note: Museum display behind glass.
